newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: FEATURE - Cambodia's press targets Pol Pot, premier.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Cambodia's press targets Pol Pot, premier.

text.p: The feisty Cambodian press has pulled no punches when describing the crimes of captured Khmer Rouge chief Pol Pot, but in the past week, withering words have not been reserved for the communist strongman.

Many local newspapers have described Cambodia's leading political figures in equally caustic terms, accusing some of raving on drugs, and others of suffering from mental illness or being worth little more than chicken excrement.
The no-holds-barred style is not unusual in Phnom Penh, where 40 local-language papers -- most with the support of rival political parties -- compete fiercely for readers.
While the war with the Khmer Rouge guerrilla group may be at an end, conflicts within the coalition government -- often played out in the press -- appear as bitter as ever, analysts said.
POLITICAL HIRED GUNS
"Most journalists here are political hired guns," said Mike Fowler, an American journalist based in Phnom Penh who is writing a book about the Cambodian newspaper business.

As First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Second Prime Minister Hun Sen prepare to face each other in elections next May, the fiercely partisan local press will be an inevitable battleground, analysts said.

Part of the reason is that the Cambodian news media, which blossomed during a United Nations-supervised peace process and election in 1993, has in many cases become dependent on the financial backing of political parties for survival, he said.

"It's very difficult to make a living as an honest, independent journalist in Cambodia, and few journalists do," Fowler said. "Some would prefer to be independent but simply can't make money without political patronage."
The result can be attacks on political figures which would never be tolerated elsewhere in the region.
For the time being, Pol Pot has drawn some -- though not all -- of the newspapers' attention away from political bickering.

"Although more than 20 years have passed, Pol Pot's hellish regime of three years, eight months and 20 days still fills the memory, fresh like yesterday, with indescribable hardship, bitterness, sadness and suffering," the Phnom Penh newspaper said in a recent edition.
POL POT CALLED A PIG
Other newspapers described Pol Pot as a "pig" but one pointed out that he still deserved a fair trial for the crimes committed during his 1975-79 "killing fields" regime.
"Pol Pot is a man. He has the full right to live and be equal -- and stand in front of the law," said Cambodia's most popular newspaper, Rasmei Kampuchea, or "Light of Cambodia".
Pol Pot "knew only violence" but he still had human rights, the paper said.
But while they remembered Pol Pot's crimes, the Phnom Penh newspapers still attack politicians.

Ranariddh -- whose party has spearheaded talks with a Khmer Rouge faction which broke with Pol Pot and detained him -- was criticised for negotiating with them in the first place. Hun Sen was accused of being indifferent to peace.
Several journalists have been murdered in recent years and there have also been grenade attacks on newspapers and a television station.
No one is ruling out more attacks but the danger is unlikely to put a damper on the slanging match being played out in the papers.

"People have knocked off journalists before, threatened them and put them in jail, but it hasn't stopped them. Their patrons can always find someone to write this stuff," said a foreign political analyst.
